name: Four thieves vinegar

card.summary: A historic herb-and-garlic infused vinegar, used as an aromatic antiseptic and skin wash, tied to plague-era hygiene.
card.aka: Vinaigre des quatre voleurs; Acetum bezoardicum; seven thieves vinegar
card.note: Historical remedy; modern use is mostly cultural.

quick.overview:
Four thieves vinegar is vinegar steeped with aromatic herbs, spices and garlic. Legend says thieves who robbed plague victims stayed healthy by using it. Historically it was rubbed on hands, face and temples as a cleansing, protective wash.

Its appearance angle is as a herbal skin and hygiene wash with a long history. Some researchers suggest the herbs repelled fleas or have antimicrobial properties; no clinical trials test it as a skin product.
quick.how: Historical recipes steep herbs such as rosemary, sage, lavender, thyme and wormwood, plus cloves and garlic, in wine or cider vinegar for days or weeks, then strain it. It was applied to the skin or used as a household cleanser and aromatic.
quick.risks: Vinegar is acidic and can irritate skin and eyes when undiluted. Some historical herbs, such as wormwood, are not benign. It was never shown to prevent plague.

lead: Four thieves vinegar is a vinegar infused with herbs, spices or garlic that was long believed to protect against plague.[1] The legend describes thieves who robbed the sick and dead without falling ill, and who traded the recipe for leniency when caught; versions are set in Marseille or Toulouse in dates ranging from the 14th to 18th centuries.[1]
It was applied to the body, especially hands, face and temples, and used as a disinfecting wash and aromatic.[2] For looks, it fits the tradition of herbal vinegar toilet waters and skin washes.
Researchers have suggested that some herbs could repel fleas or have antimicrobial activity, and a review of traditional plant remedies for pandemics discusses herbal preparations of this type.[1][3]

chain: Herb-infused vinegar used as a wash
Aromatic, mildly acidic cleansing of skin
angle.text: It was used as a cleansing, scented wash on the face and hands. Claims about disease protection are historical; no studies test it as a cosmetic.

infobox: Vinegar, rosemary, sage, lavender, thyme, garlic, cloves
Sold in Provence; the name is also used by an activist collective

paras: Typical formulas use white wine or cider vinegar with herbs such as rosemary, sage, lavender, thyme, rue, wormwood and mint, plus spices like clove and cinnamon and fresh garlic, macerated for ten to fifteen days and then strained.[2] Modern versions often use four herbs to echo the four thieves.[1]

Folklore ties it to plague outbreaks; one account places it in the 1720 Marseille plague and another in Toulouse in 1628, with a Franciscan friar as source.[2] A related sixteenth-century preparation, Acetum bezoardicum, is described as a precursor.[2] An 18th-century London anecdote mentions apothecaries displaying signs for it during a plague scare.[1] In Italy a related 'seven thieves' mixture is sold as smelling salts.[1]
No studies found. A 2020 historical-botanical review discusses traditional plant remedies used in pandemics generally.[3]
The Four Thieves Vinegar Collective is an anarchist group that publishes do-it-yourself medicine and medical-technology projects; it borrows the name and is not about the vinegar itself.[4]

timeline.event: Recipes said to be codified in pharmacopoeias.[2]

refs.title: Pandemics and Traditional Plant-Based Remedies. A Historical-Botanical Review in the Era of COVID19
